questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
One of the main reasons I chose Germany was that I wanted to improve my German. Since I study in Denmark and may want to work either in Germany or in a field involving German-Danish cooperation in the future, I saw the exchange as a good opportunity to strengthen my language skills.

I was also interested in experiencing everyday life in Germany and learning more about German culture outside of what I had encountered through language classes and previous visits. Another factor was the location of the university. I wanted to spend some time living somewhere with easier access to nature and outdoor activities than I am used to in Copenhagen.

Germany also felt like a relatively safe and accessible destination for an exchange semester. It is close to Denmark, which made travelling home manageable, while still providing the experience of living abroad. In addition, Heidelberg was particularly attractive because of its strong academic reputation. The university is one of the oldest and most well-known in Germany, and its reputation for high academic standards was an important factor in my decision.

Overall, the exchange combined several things I was looking for: language practice, insight into German society and culture, strong academic opportunities, and the chance to live in a different environment for a semester.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Overall, I would rate my study abroad experience very positively. One of the highlights was the social aspect of the exchange. I met people from many different countries, and it was interesting to get to know students with different backgrounds, perspectives, and academic interests. The international environment made it easy to meet new people and build friendships.

At the same time, some of the administrative processes were more confusing than I had expected. Information was sometimes spread across different platforms, and it could be difficult to understand which steps were required and when deadlines applied. While things generally worked out in the end, navigating the administrative side of the exchange required more independent effort than I had anticipated.

Academically, I felt challenged in a positive way. The teaching style and expectations were different from what I was used to, and studying in German required additional effort, especially at the beginning of the semester. However, this also made the experience rewarding, as I developed both academically and linguistically throughout my stay.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
Some of the information I needed upon arrival was easy to find, while other parts were more difficult to navigate. It was relatively straightforward to find information about social activities, student organizations, and opportunities to meet other international students. This made it easy to establish a social network early in the semester.

The academic side was more challenging. Information about course enrollment, deadlines, and the structure of the German university system was not always easy to find or understand. Choosing classes was particularly confusing, as the process differed significantly from what I was used to, and there were several points where I was unsure whether I had completed the necessary steps correctly. As a result, I spent quite a lot of time worrying about whether I was enrolled right and meeting the relevant deadlines.

The Erasmus introduction seminars were helpful and provided a good overview of the most important practical matters. However, I often found myself relying on other students to understand specific procedures and requirements. While peer support was valuable, I think some of this information could have been communicated more clearly through official channels.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I did receive assistance upon arrival, primarily through the Erasmus introduction seminars that took place during the first week. These sessions provided a useful overview of the Erasmus process and introduced the most important practical matters related to studying at Heidelberg University.

In addition, both the central Erasmus coordinator and my departmental coordinator were available by email and generally willing to help when I had questions. However, response times were often quite slow, which could be stressful when dealing with deadlines or administrative issues. It also took me some time to realize that there was a phone number available for direct contact, which might have helped resolve some issues more quickly.

Overall, support was available when needed, but I often felt that I had to navigate many things on my own. While the seminars provided a good starting point, I would have appreciated more accessible and responsive support during the first weeks of the semester.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer:
I was moderately satisfied with the orientation and assistance available upon arrival. The Erasmus introduction seminars were helpful and gave a good overview of the practical aspects of studying at the university. They also made it easier to meet other international students and begin building a social network.

However, I found that information regarding course selection, enrollment procedures, deadlines, and the German academic system was sometimes difficult to access or understand. In several cases, I relied on fellow students to explain processes that I felt could have been communicated more clearly through official channels. Support from coordinators was available, but response times to emails were often slow, which could make administrative issues more stressful than necessary.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
For me, finding off-campus housing was relatively easy. I started searching in August through WG-Gesucht, which I believe gave me an advantage, as many students only begin looking for accommodation in September. As a result, I was able to find a room before the main rush began.

That said, I know that the experience was not the same for everyone. Several friends had difficulty finding accommodation, particularly those who decided to extend their stay for an additional semester and had to search for housing outside the regular intake periods. Availability can therefore depend quite heavily on timing.

The room I found was significantly more expensive than the student dormitories, but this is something students should be aware of when considering private accommodation. In terms of overall cost, however, housing prices felt reasonable to me. Coming from Copenhagen, I found accommodation in Heidelberg to be comparatively affordable, although perceptions of pricing will naturally depend on a student's home country and financial situation.

My recommendation would be to start searching as early as possible and to use platforms such as WG-Gesucht. Students who are flexible regarding location and housing type will likely have an easier time finding a place to live.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Heidelberg is a relatively small city, so areas outside the Altstadt, such as Pfaffengrund, Rohrbach, and other residential neighbourhoods, can feel quite suburban compared to the city centre. However, this is also where much of the available housing is located, and I found the quieter atmosphere to be a benefit rather than a drawback. Living outside the centre can also be a good way to get to know people who are already established in the city, especially if you live in a shared apartment with local students or long-term residents.

One thing future exchange students should keep in mind is that distances in Heidelberg are generally short. A 20-minute bike ride from the Altstadt takes you surprisingly far, and cycling is often the fastest and most convenient way to get around. Because of this, I would not limit my housing search to the city centre.

I would also recommend not worrying too much if you do not find the perfect accommodation immediately. Many students spend a lot of time comparing neighbourhoods before arriving, but after a few weeks in Heidelberg I found that most parts of the city were well connected and easy to reach. Being open-minded about location can make the housing search much less stressful.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall, I was satisfied with the housing available to students. While finding accommodation can require some planning and flexibility, especially for students arriving at the start of the semester, I found that there were enough options available through student residences and the private housing market.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I found the registration process relatively manageable, although not entirely straightforward. Most of the necessary information was available, and I was ultimately able to complete all required steps without major problems. However, there were several administrative procedures that were unfamiliar to me, and it was not always clear in which order different tasks needed to be completed.

The most challenging part was often knowing whom to contact when questions arose. As an exchange student, it was sometimes unclear whether a particular issue should be addressed to my home university or to Heidelberg University. This occasionally led to delays, as I would need to wait for responses before understanding who was responsible for a given part of the process.

Overall, the process worked well, but it required a degree of independence and persistence. Once I became familiar with the system, it was much easier to navigate, but the initial learning curve was steeper than I had expected.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The registration process was explained through a series of detailed emails sent by the university before the semester began. These emails outlined the necessary steps, including enrolment in the university's digital systems, payment of semester fees, and the procedure for obtaining a student card. I found the instructions generally clear and comprehensive.

After completing the online registration steps, I had to collect my student card in person from a university building. This process was straightforward and did not take much time. While there were quite a few administrative steps overall, the university provided sufficient information to complete them successfully.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
The primary form of support was through email communication with the International Office, Erasmus coordinators, and departmental coordinators. Most questions could be addressed this way, although response times sometimes varied depending on the issue and the time of year.

Students could also contact the university by phone or visit the International Office in person if needed. While I mainly relied on email, it was reassuring to know that other forms of support were available. In addition, the Erasmus orientation events provided opportunities to ask questions and receive guidance on practical and academic matters during the first weeks of the semester.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
I was partially successful in registering for the classes I wanted. I was able to enroll in most of the courses that fit my study plan, but there were a few limitations that affected the final result.

One issue was that I was not aware until quite late in the process that a German language course at B2 level or above could potentially be accredited at master's level. By the time I learned this, my course selection was already largely settled, and I ended up taking an additional course that I would probably have planned differently otherwise.

I was also somewhat disappointed that there were no master's courses in my field taught in German; the relevant courses were offered only in English. Since one of my goals was to improve my German through academic study, I had hoped for more opportunities to take subject-related courses in German.

Overall, I was able to register for enough courses to complete my semester successfully, but my final course selection was not exactly what I had originally hoped for.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
My main advice would be not to panic if the registration process initially feels confusing. The German system is less rigid than the one at the University of Copenhagen, and there is often more flexibility than it first appears. In many cases, you can register for several classes, attend the first sessions, and then decide which courses are the best fit for your interests and study requirements.

I would also recommend reaching out to professors and departmental coordinators if you are unsure about anything. In my experience, they were very patient and understanding towards Erasmus students and were generally willing to help clarify requirements and course options.

Finally, I would suggest talking to other exchange students early on. Some of the most useful information I received came from students who had already gone through the same process. Even if it feels like everyone else understands the system better than you do, most people are figuring it out as they go along.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Overall, I was satisfied with the academic programme at my host institution. The courses were academically relevant, and I appreciated being exposed to different teaching styles and perspectives than those I am used to at my home university. Studying in a different academic environment was one of the most valuable parts of the exchange.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I found the academic level of the courses to be very comparable to what I am used to at my home university. The expectations regarding preparation, participation, and independent thinking were appropriate for a master's student, and I generally felt well prepared for the coursework.

I primarily took seminar-based courses, which meant that a large part of the learning took place through discussion and active participation. I enjoyed this format, as it allowed students to engage directly with the course material and with each other's perspectives.

One difference I noticed was that there seemed to be a greater amount of mandatory coursework throughout the semester. Compared to my experience at the University of Copenhagen, there were more assignments, presentations, and written submissions that had to be completed during the course. While this required more continuous work, it also helped maintain engagement with the material throughout the semester.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
I found the teaching style at my host institution to be very similar to that of UCPH. The courses emphasized independent reading, critical discussion, and active participation from students. In the seminars I attended, students were expected to engage with the literature and contribute to discussions rather than simply listen to lectures.

One difference was that there appeared to be more mandatory assignments and coursework throughout the semester. However, the overall academic culture, expectations regarding student independence, and the relationship between students and professors felt quite familiar to me. As a result, I found it relatively easy to adapt to the teaching style at Heidelberg University.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.answer:

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend that future exchange students choose courses based on their interests rather than focusing too heavily on course titles alone. In my experience, seminar-based courses were particularly rewarding because they encouraged discussion and allowed students to engage closely with both the material and their classmates.

I would also recommend taking a German language course, especially for students who plan to stay in Germany for an extended period or who would like to improve their language skills alongside their academic studies. Even for students whose degree programme is taught primarily in English, a language course can make everyday life and social interactions much easier.

More generally, I would encourage future exchange students to take advantage of the flexibility of the German system and attend a few different courses at the beginning of the semester before making final decisions. This makes it easier to find courses that match both academic interests and preferred teaching styles.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
One expense that was significantly lower than I expected was transportation. The Deutschlandticket was excellent value for money. For €65 per month, it provided access to regional and local public transport across Germany, which made it possible to travel extensively without spending much on transportation. It gave me a great deal of flexibility throughout the semester.

I also found groceries to be somewhat cheaper than what I am used to in Copenhagen, especially when shopping at discount supermarkets. This made everyday living costs more manageable than I had anticipated.

Eating out was another pleasant surprise. Restaurants, cafés, and student bars were generally much cheaper than their equivalents in Copenhagen, which made it easier to socialize and explore the city without worrying too much about costs.

Finally, I was impressed by the affordability of cultural and leisure activities. Student discounts were widely available, and many museums, events, and attractions could be visited at a relatively low cost. This made it easier to take advantage of opportunities outside of my studies throughout the semester.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not really engage in any of them

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There were many cultural, athletic, and social activities available to students. One of the main opportunities was Hochschulsport, the university sports programme, which offers a wide range of sports and fitness activities at affordable prices. However, future students should be aware that popular courses fill up very quickly, so it is important to be ready when registration opens.

In addition to university activities, there were many opportunities to participate in social and cultural life through student organizations, Erasmus events, and local initiatives. Heidelberg has a large student population, which means there is usually something happening, whether it is a cultural event, a language exchange, or a social gathering.

I would also note that many good options exist outside the university itself. There are numerous sports clubs, gyms, hiking groups, and cultural associations in the city that are open to students. In my experience, students should not limit themselves to university activities, as some of the best opportunities to meet people and become part of the local community can be found outside the university as well.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would strongly recommend taking advantage of the natural surroundings of Heidelberg. The city is located close to forests, hills, and hiking trails, and spending time outdoors was one of the highlights of my stay. Philosophenweg is particularly worth visiting, especially around sunset, as it offers a beautiful view over the city and the Neckar River.

I would also encourage students to explore other cities in the region. Mannheim, Frankfurt, and Karlsruhe are all easily accessible by public transport and offer a different atmosphere from Heidelberg, including a wider range of nightlife, cultural events, and concerts. For students interested in clubbing, these cities provide more options than Heidelberg itself.

Another recommendation would be to visit Baden-Baden. The town is known for its thermal baths and spas, which can be a nice break from studying and travelling. More generally, I would encourage students to use the Deutschlandticket to explore as much of the region as possible. Some of my best experiences during the semester came from day trips and spontaneous weekends away rather than planned university activities.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I would strongly recommend taking advantage of the natural surroundings of Heidelberg. The city is located close to forests, hills, and hiking trails, and spending time outdoors was one of the highlights of my stay. For students interested in clubbing, these cities provide more options than Heidelberg itself.

More generally, I would encourage students to use the Deutschlandticket to explore as much of the region as possible. Some of my best experiences during the semester came from day trips and spontaneous weekends away rather than planned university activities.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
I found it relatively easy to adjust to the local culture. Coming from Denmark, there were many similarities in terms of social norms, daily life, and expectations within the university environment. As a result, there were few situations in which I felt significant culture shock.

Of course, there were some differences in communication styles, administrative procedures, and university traditions, but these were generally easy to adapt to over time. Having some prior knowledge of the German language also made everyday interactions easier and helped me feel more comfortable in my surroundings. At the same time, speaking a foreign language inevitably leads to misunderstandings from time to time. There were occasions where I expressed myself awkwardly or misunderstood a social situation because of language limitations, which could be a little embarrassing, but this was also a natural part of the learning process.

Overall, I found Heidelberg to be a welcoming and accessible place to live, and I adjusted to life there fairly quickly.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
My main advice would be not to be discouraged if local students switch to English when speaking with you. In many cases, they are simply trying to be helpful or make the conversation easier, rather than signaling that your German is not good enough.

If your goal is to improve your German, it is worth politely continuing in German when possible. In my experience, German students were generally patient and supportive when I made mistakes or needed extra time to express myself. Learning a language inevitably involves awkward moments and misunderstandings, but most people were understanding and appreciated the effort.

I would also recommend joining student activities, sports clubs, or language exchanges where repeated contact makes it easier to build friendships over time. Like anywhere else, social connections tend to develop more naturally when you see the same people regularly rather than only meeting them at one-off events.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
To be honest, I did not find any cultural differences particularly challenging. One reason for this is that, as an exchange student, you are somewhat sheltered from many of the difficulties that people might otherwise face when moving to a new country. Much of your social life revolves around other international students who are going through the same experience, and there are support structures in place to help you navigate practical issues.

Germany and Denmark are also relatively similar in many respects, which made everyday life easy to adapt to. While there were small differences in communication styles, university administration, and social customs, these were generally minor and easy to adjust to over time.

As a result, I experienced the cultural differences more as opportunities to learn than as challenges that created significant difficulties in daily life.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
There were several aspects of German culture that I particularly appreciated during my stay. One was the nightlife and social culture. Heidelberg itself has a lively student environment, and its location also made it easy to visit larger nearby cities with a wider range of cultural events, concerts, and nightlife.

I also appreciated the cultural diversity that characterizes modern Germany. Throughout the semester, I met people from many different backgrounds, and I found it interesting to experience a society where different cultures and traditions coexist in everyday life.

Another aspect I enjoyed was the connection to nature. It was easy to spend time outdoors, whether through hiking, cycling, or simply walking in the surrounding hills and forests. Having access to nature so close to the city contributed greatly to my quality of life during the exchange.

Finally, I was impressed by the care many people seemed to take of their possessions and public spaces. Whether it was maintaining bicycles, looking after historic buildings, or participating in recycling and environmental initiatives, I often felt there was a culture of stewardship and long-term thinking that I found both admirable and inspiring.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) The course registration is way different than the one we are used to
2) Find friends, talk to as many as possible and you will find a home in Heidelberg you never want to leave
3) Visit a German course in Max Weber Haus

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
My main advice would be to make the most of the experience while you are there. An exchange semester passes surprisingly quickly, and it is easy to become so focused on coursework, deadlines, and administrative requirements that you forget to enjoy the opportunity itself.

Of course, academic responsibilities are important, but I would encourage future students to leave room for spontaneity as well. Take day trips, join social events, spend time with friends, and explore places that are not on any official university programme. Some of my most memorable experiences came from activities outside the classroom.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was undoubtedly the people I met and the friendships I formed during the semester. Living and studying alongside students from many different countries created connections that would have been difficult to make under ordinary circumstances. Some of these friendships became an important part of my daily life and greatly shaped my experience abroad.

What makes these relationships particularly meaningful is that they are tied to a unique period of life that can never quite be repeated. Long after I have forgotten the details of individual courses or administrative procedures, I expect to remember the conversations, shared experiences, and people I met during my time in Heidelberg. For me, those personal connections are the most valuable thing I gained from the exchange and the part of the experience that will stay with me the longest.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
The greatest challenge for me was learning to be comfortable with uncertainty. Before and during the first part of the exchange, there were many things I did not know: whether I had chosen the right courses, whether I understood the administrative requirements correctly, whether my German would be sufficient, and what my social life would look like in a new country.

Many of these concerns eventually resolved themselves, but at the time they could feel quite overwhelming. Looking back, I think the challenge was less about any specific practical problem and more about accepting that not everything can be planned or controlled in advance.

At the same time, this turned out to be one of the most valuable aspects of the experience. Being placed in unfamiliar situations forced me to become more adaptable and confident in my ability to figure things out as I went along. By the end of the semester, I was much more comfortable navigating uncertainty than I had been at the beginning.
